siteSettings.heroThesis: I'm a product person. I keep asking why until the real problem shows up, then I build what fixes it and stay to make sure it works. At QShop I lead product, helping 59,700+ businesses sell online and on WhatsApp. At Yoke Solutions (YSL) I lead platforms for government and business, like the NCC website and Ekiti State's jobs platform.
siteSettings.problemLead: Ask why until the real problem shows up.
siteSettings.problemBody: I talk to users and the people who serve them. Where do they get stuck? What are they still doing by hand? What is it costing them? Often the real problem is not the one in the request. At QNotify, real order data showed the problem was much smaller than everyone assumed, so we changed direction.
siteSettings.betLead: Test the answer early, then build it properly.
siteSettings.betBody: I sketch, prototype, and test with real people before a team spends months on something. Then I write the plan and lead the build. That is how QShop cut onboarding drop-off from 70% to 45%, and how the NCC got a new website it formally accepted.
siteSettings.outcomeLead: Launch is the start. I stay to see what happens next.
siteSettings.aboutHero: Start with the user's problem. [Build the business around it.]
siteSettings.aboutOrigin:
My route into product started in agriculture and operations. I studied Agricultural Administration, then became COO at MyFarmbase Africa, helping scale an EdTech and agribusiness platform to 9,000+ active users across West Africa and supporting the launch of 200+ profitable agribusinesses. Automating training workflows reduced administrative overhead by over 50%.

That experience still shapes how I work: understand the people, map the process, find where the system breaks, and build what fixes it. Today I do that as Product Lead at QShop, as Lead Project Manager for government and enterprise platforms at Yoke Solutions, and in the programmes and tools I build on my own time.
siteSettings.aboutOperatingInstinct:
I enjoy sitting with users, understanding their problems, and turning what I learn into a direction the team can act on. I connect that discovery to business priorities, scoped plans, and prototypes that make decisions easier.

Delivery is part of that responsibility. I work with founders, engineers, designers, and client stakeholders to set priorities, manage scope, and keep work moving. Sometimes the right decision is a better activation flow; sometimes it is self-service tooling that removes recurring work; sometimes it is stopping an idea whose dependencies do not add up.
siteSettings.aboutCommunity: As Programme Lead for Morph by TNX Solve, I run a six-week product-building programme for teenagers: sessions, community managers, participant communications, Demo Day, and safeguarding as the Designated Safeguarding Lead. I also facilitated an AI and no-code train-the-trainer workshop for Global Shapers Ota Hub in April 2026, taking participants from problem definition to working prototypes. Since January 2026 I have served on the board of Adlai Heroes Foundation, advising on programme strategy, operations, and digital products.

qshop.name: QShop Tech
qshop.coverAlt: The QShop homepage: an online store and WhatsApp checkout in one setup
qshop.tagline: Helping 59,700+ businesses sell online and on WhatsApp.

sections.label: Context
sections.body: QShop helps businesses sell in two places at once: their own online store, and WhatsApp. I joined as Product Manager in June 2022 and became Product Lead in April 2024. The platform serves 59,700+ registered stores, 18,000+ monthly orders, and $5.2M in annual GMV. Those figures describe the scale I work at; the results I drove directly are on the pages that follow.

sections.label: Questions I keep asking
sections.body: Where do new merchants give up? What are they still doing by hand that the product could do for them? If we could only say yes to one request this month, which one would help the most stores? Most of the work on these pages started with one of those questions.

sections.label: Roadmap
sections.body: I sequence the roadmap across several streams at once. One July plan lined up eight pieces of work in a single fortnight: storefront themes, a one-page checkout, simpler shipping setup, QNotify, an inactivity prompt, and smaller fixes. Multi-branch inventory was designed and prototyped, then explicitly deprioritised in that plan so checkout and shipping could go first.

sections.label: Operations
sections.body: I extended the admin so internal teams could handle five recurring request types themselves, taking that work off the support and engineering queues.

sections.label: Team
sections.body: I report to the founder and manage an associate PM. Setting sprint priorities with engineering lifted delivery throughput by about 30%.

qshop-activation.name: QShop · Onboarding & activation
qshop-activation.tagline: Getting more new merchants from sign-up to a working store and a first sale.

sections.label: The question
sections.body: Why were 70% of new merchants signing up and never finishing their store?

sections.label: Getting to the root
sections.body: I looked at exactly where people stopped and asked what each step demanded of them. For every drop-off point I wrote down a guess about the cause, then tested changes one at a time to see which guesses held.

sections.label: Result
sections.body: Onboarding drop-off fell from 70% to 45%, and new merchants reached their first sale 15% faster. I also launched promotion and discovery features that increased order volume at store level.

sections.label: Still looking for gaps
sections.body: The work continues. A recent audit found merchants could launch a store with no shipping set up, leaving customers stuck at checkout. I wrote a ranked fix list for engineering and put simpler shipping setup and a one-page checkout on the roadmap.

qnotify.name: QNotify
qnotify.coverAlt: The QNotify page: WhatsApp follow-ups that bring customers back
qnotify.tagline: Testing an assumption against real order data before building on it.

sections.label: The bet
sections.body: QNotify began as a WhatsApp tool to recover abandoned orders for QShop merchants, built on the common assumption that most online carts are abandoned.

sections.label: The question
sections.body: Before building further, I asked a simple question: how many orders are really abandoned? I analysed 2,506 real orders from a pilot store. Recent abandonment was 1.6%, and 3.2 to 6.2% historically. Recovery alone would have added about one extra order a week.

sections.label: The decision
sections.body: That shifted the focus to campaigns merchants can send themselves, such as restock alerts, repeat-purchase nudges, and promotions, with abandoned-order recovery kept as one flow of four message templates. The pilot runs across 25 QShop stores.

sections.label: Guardrails
sections.body: Success is measured on merchants activated, recovery lift, and revenue per merchant, with a 95% WhatsApp delivery floor so the sending number is never put at risk. Open questions: whether 1.6% holds across the other 24 stores, and whether to price per message or per recovered sale.

features.name: Orders analysed
features.detail: One pilot store, real order history.

features.name: Real abandonment
features.detail: Far below the assumed rate, which changed the plan.

features.name: Pilot
features.detail: Fashion, household, and skincare merchants.

features.name: Delivery floor
features.detail: Protects the sending number from being blocked.

ncc.coverAlt: The redesigned Nigerian Communications Commission homepage
ncc.tagline: Rebuilding the Nigerian Communications Commission's website around what the public comes for.

sections.label: Context
sections.body: The Nigerian Communications Commission's website was outdated, hard to use on mobile, and had outgrown its structure. The Commission also needed incident reporting and an events calendar.

sections.label: The question
sections.body: What do people actually come to the NCC website for, and why was it so hard to find? We answered that before designing anything.

sections.label: Discovery
sections.body: We ran three stakeholder workshops and audited 400+ legacy pages using analytics data, then restructured the information around what visitors look for. Seven design concepts went to review and three were shortlisted.

sections.label: Delivery
sections.body: I led a five-person cross-functional team through design, build, security hardening, and testing. 58 defects were logged in testing, and none rated critical or high were outstanding at sign-off.

sections.label: Handover
sections.body: We trained NCC staff to run the site themselves and handed over manuals and publishing workflows. The Commission formally accepted the work in April 2025: all 16 contractual scope items delivered on schedule, with agreed UX and accessibility acceptance scores up 50%.

kalife-travels.tagline: Rebuilding a 50-year-old travel agency's flight booking after two failed attempts.

sections.label: The question
sections.body: Two earlier rebuilds had failed. Why? The obvious answer was the software. The real answer was underneath it.

sections.label: The root cause
sections.body: Kalife sold flights through an entry-level airline booking connection that only showed public fares and was being shut down in July 2026. No rebuild on top of it could work. I diagnosed the limit, wrote the proposal to move to an enterprise tier, and planned a phased rebuild: a new booking platform plus a back office where Kalife sets its own markups and airline commissions.

sections.label: What is built
sections.body: Multi-carrier flight search, fare and baggage details, multi-city booking, payments, ticketing, booking management, and a tour catalogue. 25 airline commission rules are set up and back-office testing has passed.

sugar-guest-pro.name: Sugar Guest Pro

sections.label: The question
sections.body: Event planners manage guest lists and check-ins across spreadsheets and chats. Would a WhatsApp-based flow fit how they actually work, or just add another tool?

sections.label: What I did
sections.body: I interviewed planners and ran quick WhatsApp experiments to validate the key workflows before committing to a bigger build.

sections.label: Now
sections.body: The product is in keep-the-lights-on mode: I keep it running while focus sits elsewhere, with more attention planned later.

sections.label: Lesson
sections.body: Message delivery on WhatsApp is less reliable than it looks. Meta's rules and mobile carriers both affect whether a message arrives, and a product built on them absorbs that risk. It now shapes how the next phase will be planned.

impactops.name: Adlai ImpactOps

qtrack.tagline: Knowing when to stop: what 500+ users taught me about a WhatsApp expense tracker.

sections.label: The question
sections.body: Could tracking expenses on WhatsApp make the habit easier to keep? QTrack was a Yoke Solutions (YSL) product built to find out.

sections.label: What I tested
sections.body: I validated the product with 500+ users, looking at what it would take for people to keep using it, not just try it.

sections.label: Getting to the root
sections.body: Sustained use depended on a big change in behaviour and on bank connections that were not viable. The early sign-ups did not answer either question.

sections.label: Decision
sections.body: I recommended stopping, and we discontinued it. The lesson: a user count is not validation until you know what keeps people coming back.

features.name: Early adoption
features.detail: Tested a WhatsApp expense-tracking product with real users.

features.name: Investment decision
features.detail: Stopped the initiative after identifying behavioural and bank-API dependencies.

claude-skills.name: Prototyping with AI
claude-skills.tagline: How I test product ideas in working software before a team commits.

sections.label: The question
sections.body: What is the fastest way to find out if an idea is right? Often it is to build a rough version and put it in front of real people.

sections.label: How I do it
sections.body: I use AI coding agents to turn an idea into something people can click in days, not weeks. I have set them up to keep context between sessions, hand work over cleanly to engineers, and check quality and security as they go.

sections.label: Where it shows
sections.body: It is how I prototyped QShop's multi-branch inventory and checkout ideas, built the Morph Ops app, and shaped the Lagos Innovates programme sites and this portfolio, working with engineers on the parts that need them.

sections.label: What it means for teams
sections.body: Fewer debates about what we think users want, and more evidence from what they actually do, before engineering time is committed.

features.name: Speed
features.detail: From idea to something people can use.

features.name: Evidence
features.detail: Decisions made on what users do.

features.name: Handover
features.detail: Prototypes become clear specs.

fof-ops.name: FOF Ops
fof-ops.summary: Leading a church's move to digital
fof-ops.tagline: Making sure no one who joins the church's foundation programme falls through the cracks.

sections.label: Context
sections.body: Foundation of Faith (FOF) is my church's programme for people joining the church. I am leading the move from paper and spreadsheets to one system.

sections.label: The question
sections.body: How do you make sure nobody who starts the programme quietly drops out, and that everyone who finishes finds a place to serve?

sections.label: Rules first
sections.body: Before building, I agreed the programme rules with church leadership: what counts as completing, when someone needs attention, what each support person records every week, and how new members join a church department.

sections.label: What it does
sections.body: Participants see their week, duties, and updates. Support people track attendance, group meetings, and follow-ups for their group. Leaders see who needs attention, who has completed, and who has joined a department.

features.name: Rules
features.detail: Completion, attention, and weekly records.

features.name: Three sides
features.detail: Each sees what they need.

features.name: Follow-through
features.detail: Tracked from choice to joined.

nepa-trackr.name: NEPA Trackr
nepa-trackr.tagline: Turning a daily frustration with power supply into evidence.

sections.label: The question
sections.body: How often does my street in Ikorodu actually have power? Everyone had a feeling. Nobody had the numbers to take to the electricity company.

sections.label: What I built
sections.body: A one-tap app to log when power goes off and comes back, a 24-hour timeline of supply, and an analysis that finds patterns and drafts points for a formal complaint. It installs on a phone like an app.

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.body: A complaint backed by a log of every outage is much harder to ignore than one based on memory.

features.name: Logging
features.detail: Power off, power back.

features.name: Timeline
features.detail: See supply patterns at a glance.

features.name: Analysis
features.detail: Patterns and talking points for a formal letter.

budget-tracker.name: Budget Track
budget-tracker.tagline: A budget that keeps itself up to date.

sections.label: The question
sections.body: Why do budgets fall apart? Because typing in every transaction is tedious, so people stop.

sections.label: What I built
sections.body: It reads my bank alert emails, records each transaction, and sorts it into budget pockets automatically, so I know when I am close to or over budget without typing anything in.

sections.label: Details
sections.body: Private to me, built for my phone, and careful never to count the same transaction twice.

features.name: Input
features.detail: No manual entry.

features.name: Sorting
features.detail: Each transaction lands in a budget.

features.name: Alerts
features.detail: I know before the month runs out.

sections.label: Why I built it
sections.body: My niece Miracle was born prematurely. While she was in care, our family needed a simple way to record her readings and see how she was doing over time, instead of scattered numbers.

sections.label: What it did
sections.body: A phone-first app anyone in the family could open: quick entry for her urine output, temperature, and nappies, with output worked out per kilogram per hour and charts that showed the trend.

sections.label: In memory
sections.body: Miracle lived for five days. I will always remember and cherish her. May she rest in peace.
